ocar.opportunity: Neuronal circuits are the target of both evolutionary and individual adaptation. Mapping them at synaptic resolution across animals would reveal how brains implement navigation, prediction, and environmental shaping over phylogeny and ontogeny.
ocar.challenge: Accessible synaptic-resolution volumes have grown, but centimetre-scale targets—local circuits of larger brains including human, and a whole adult mouse brain—still face bottlenecks in tissue preparation, ablation or sectioning, imaging, and AI-based 3D analysis.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2025), reviews two decades of large-scale 3D electron microscopy and machine learning that expanded connectomically accessible synaptic volumes by a factor of 1,000, from about 100 µm³ to about 1 mm³, and discusses remaining challenges plus the prospect of connectomic screening.
ocar.resolution: The review argues the field can now move beyond specialized miniature circuits to a large range of local mouse neuropil, including cortical grey matter. Next major targets named are local cortical circuits of larger brains (including human) and whole-brain synaptic connectomes of small reptiles, rodents, birds, and non-human primates. The same frontier methods are said to enable multifold mapping of smaller circuits for screening of evolution, experience, behaviour, aging, and pathology.
ocar.future_work: Remaining challenges are highlighted especially for centimetre-scale mapping such as a whole adult mouse brain. Connectomic screening of evolutionary determinism, individual experience, behavioural performance, and age-dependent or pathological alterations is presented as the implied use of smaller-circuit mapping.

summaries.beginner: Mapping every synapse in a piece of brain has gotten about a thousand times larger over twenty years, from a speck to about a cubic millimetre. This review argues we can now map local mouse circuits and should next aim at bigger brains, while using smaller circuits as a screening tool.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2025), Helmstaedter reviews synaptic-resolution connectomics. He states that large-scale 3D electron microscopy and machine learning expanded accessible volumes from about 100 µm³ to about 1 mm³ (a 1,000-fold increase), enough to move beyond miniature circuits to local mouse neuropil including cortical grey matter. He discusses innovations in tissue preparation, ablation or sectioning, imaging, and AI-based 3D analysis, and flags centimetre-scale targets such as a whole adult mouse brain. The review also positions multifold mapping of smaller circuits as a route to connectomic screening of evolution, experience, behaviour, aging, and pathology.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not name specific methods, datasets, or error rates; the 1,000-fold volume claim and the 100 µm³ to 1 mm³ bounds are the only quantitative statements given. Whole-mouse-brain mapping and screening are stated as targets, not as results of this review.

plain_language_summary: Mapping every synapse in a piece of brain has gotten about a thousand times larger over twenty years, from a speck to about a cubic millimetre. This review argues we can now map local mouse circuits and should next aim at bigger brains, while using smaller circuits as a screening tool.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric reconstructions now yield cellular-resolution synaptic networks in fruit fly, mouse, and human, opening a chance to quantify shared organizing principles of connectomes in physical space.
ocar.challenge: Physical constraints—pairwise distances or contactomes—strongly shape wiring, and neuron positions look highly optimal relative to neighbors, yet space alone cannot capture topology such as the broad degree distribution, and the degree sequence alone cannot recover spatial structure.
ocar.action: Salova and Kovács, in Network Neuroscience (2024), construct contactomes (networks of neurons in physical contact) alongside synaptic connectomes for fruit fly, mouse, and human, then fit scalable maximum-entropy generative models that combine topological constraints with spatial or contact constraints.
ocar.resolution: Joint models resolve the mismatch. Among models listed in the extract, those using the degree sequence plus a contact constraint (k+c) achieve the highest log-likelihood of the empirical connectome in fly, mouse, and human. The generative models are reported to capture additional features not used as constraints, including synaptic weights and graphlet statistics.
ocar.future_work: The extract is truncated after the introduction into supplementary tables, so later-section limitations are not available. Implied next tests are whether the same joint spatial–topological maximum-entropy recipe holds on other reconstructions and whether predicted weights and graphlets remain out-of-sample.

summaries.beginner: Wiring in fly, mouse, and human brains is shaped both by which cells touch and by how many partners each cell has. This paper shows that you need both kinds of rule—space and connection count—to rebuild a realistic network.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Network Neuroscience (2024), Salova and Kovács compare synaptic connectomes and contactomes in fruit fly, mouse, and human. They report that neuron positions are highly optimal in neighbor distance, but spatial constraints alone miss topology such as the broad degree distribution, while the degree sequence alone misses spatial structure. Scalable maximum-entropy models that combine both constraint types are said to predict additional properties including synaptic weights and graphlet statistics. Supplementary tables in the extract rank models; k+c (degree sequence plus contact) has the highest listed log-likelihood in all three organisms.
summaries.advanced: The PDF extract is truncated: introduction plus supplementary tables, without a captured discussion. AUC-ROC/PR and log-likelihood values in the supplementary tables should be checked against the full paper rather than treated as a complete results narrative. “Shared organizing principles” is an authorship framing. Out-of-sample predictive power for weights and graphlets is asserted in the abstract, but the extract does not show those analyses.

plain_language_summary: Wiring in fly, mouse, and human brains is shaped both by which cells touch and by how many partners each cell has. This paper shows that you need both kinds of rule—space and connection count—to rebuild a realistic network.

ocar.opportunity: Pairing a complete C. elegans connectome with brain-wide activity maps could test how anatomical wiring relates to global neuronal dynamics.
ocar.challenge: The structure–function relationship at whole-nervous-system scale remains unsolved: it is unclear which graph features actually predict functional correlations.
ocar.action: Uzel, Kato, and Zimmer, in Current Biology (2022), systematically compare graph features in the C. elegans connectome with correlations in nervous system–wide neuronal dynamics, and test the role of hub neurons by inhibition.
ocar.resolution: Few local connectivity motifs, and mostly non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarities, predict functional relationships between neurons. Connection strength and amount of common inputs do not improve these predictions, suggesting that topology is sufficient. Hub neurons are key to the relevant graph features; inhibiting multiple hubs specifically disrupts brain-wide correlations.
ocar.future_work: The abstract proposes that a set of hub neurons and non-local connectivity features provide an anatomical substrate for global brain dynamics; it does not specify further experiments.

summaries.beginner: In the roundworm, which cells fire together is not well predicted by who sits next to whom. This study finds that a few well-connected hub cells and longer-range wiring patterns better explain whole-brain activity.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022), Uzel, Kato, and Zimmer compare C. elegans connectome graph features with nervous system–wide activity correlations. They report that local motifs add little, whereas non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarity predict functional relationships; connection strength and common-input counts do not improve predictions. Hub neurons are described as central to those features, and inhibiting multiple hubs specifically disrupts brain-wide correlations.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not name which hubs were inhibited, how many animals were used, or quantitative prediction scores. “Topology is sufficient” is the authors’ interpretation of the strength and common-input result, not a demonstration that weights never matter.

plain_language_summary: In the roundworm, which cells fire together is not well predicted by who sits next to whom. This study finds that a few well-connected hub cells and longer-range wiring patterns better explain whole-brain activity.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse and human cortex share molecular homology, but whether local synaptic circuits have evolved is untested. That matters for using mouse as a model and for theories that rest on inhibitory-to-excitatory balance.
ocar.challenge: Human cortex has about 1,000 times more neurons than mouse and a reported increase in interneuron fraction; it is unknown how that changes local circuit architecture. Epilepsy-surgery tissue is a confound, so nonepileptic access-path biopsies matter.
ocar.action: Loomba, Straehle, Gangadharan, Heike, Khalifa, Motta, Ju, Sievers, Gempt, Meyer, and Helmstaedter, in Science (2022), used three-dimensional electron microscopy to compare connectomes from mouse, macaque, and human cortical samples, including nonepileptic neurosurgical access-path tissue.
ocar.resolution: An about 2.5-fold increase in interneurons in human versus mouse was compensated by changed axonal connection probabilities, so pyramidal-cell inhibitory-versus-excitatory input balance was not commensurately increased. Increased inhibition instead expanded an interneuron-to-interneuron network (about 10-fold), via expansion of interneuron-targeting types and higher selectivity for interneuron innervation. Total synaptic input to pyramidal cells rose modestly from about 12,000 in mouse to about 15,000 in human. The catalog abstract cites five mouse, two macaque, and two human connectomes totaling about 1.6 million synapses.
ocar.future_work: Whether the expanded interneuron-to-interneuron network comes from expansion of existing types or new subtypes requires further study. The authors encourage detailed analysis of this network component in health and disease.

summaries.beginner: Human cortex has far more neurons than mouse cortex, including more inhibitory cells, but the main excitatory cells still get a similar mix of excitation and inhibition. The extra inhibition mostly goes into a larger network of inhibitory cells talking to each other.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2022), Loomba and colleagues compared 3D electron-microscopy connectomes from mouse, macaque, and human cortex. They report an about 2.5-fold expansion of the interneuron pool in macaque and human versus mouse that does not substantially change inhibitory-to-excitatory balance onto pyramidal cells. Instead they describe a roughly 10-fold expansion of an interneuron-to-interneuron network, with bipolar-type interneurons increasing preference for other interneurons. Total pyramidal input is given as about 12,000 synapses in mouse versus about 15,000 in human. The catalog abstract cites five mouse, two macaque, and two human datasets totaling about 1.6 million synapses, using nonepileptic surgical access tissue.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Sample sizes are two human individuals, one macaque, and five mouse connectomes as stated; the abstract does not give per-layer statistics or error bars. A Science blurb’s “three times more interneurons” phrasing conflicts with the 2.5-fold figure in the main abstract; this card uses 2.5-fold. Human tissue is neurosurgical access path, not healthy volunteer cortex.

plain_language_summary: Human cortex has far more neurons than mouse cortex, including more inhibitory cells, but the main excitatory cells still get a similar mix of excitation and inhibition. The extra inhibition mostly goes into a larger network of inhibitory cells talking to each other.

ocar.opportunity: Large projects in genomics and astronomy are influential because shared, data-rich resources enable continuously arising new questions. A synaptic map of a mouse brain could play an analogous role for circuit function.
ocar.challenge: The circuits underlying brain function are complicated and have been hard to analyze at the level of synapses.
ocar.action: Abbott, Bock, Callaway, Denk, Dulac, Fairhall, Fiete, Harris, Helmstaedter, Jain, Kasthuri, LeCun, Lichtman, Littlewood, Luo, Maunsell, Reid, Rosen, Rubin, Sejnowski, Seung, Svoboda, Tank, Tsao, and Essen, in Cell (2020), discuss benefits of mapping a mouse brain at the level of synapses.
ocar.resolution: They argue that advances in automated mapping of synaptic connections make those circuits ripe for analysis, analogously to genomics and astronomy projects that enable investigation of new questions from the same data-rich sources.
ocar.future_work: The abstract is a perspective on benefits, not a methods roadmap; the implied next step is actually mapping a mouse brain at synaptic resolution.

summaries.beginner: Big shared maps in genetics and astronomy keep answering new questions. This commentary argues that a synapse-level map of a mouse brain could do the same for neuroscience.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell (2020), Abbott and a large consortium analogize connectomics to genomics and astronomy: influential not because they answer one question but because they enable many. They argue that automated mapping of synaptic connections has advanced enough that the circuits underlying brain function are ripe for analysis, and they discuss benefits of mapping a mouse brain at synapse level.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The short abstract does not specify imaging modality, cost, timeline, or biological findings. It is a perspective, not a dataset paper.

plain_language_summary: Big shared maps in genetics and astronomy keep answering new questions. This commentary argues that a synapse-level map of a mouse brain could do the same for neuroscience.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroscience now generates data volumes that outpace most biomedical fields. Within that flood, electron-microscopy connectomics is an especially hard analysis problem.
ocar.challenge: Current machine learning for EM still needs excessive labelled data while using only a small fraction of available raw images. Mapping a human brain at nanoscale would be formidable under that constraint.
ocar.action: Motta, Schurr, Staffler, and Helmstaedter, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), review how information content and analysis challenge mark EM-based connectomics as especially hard, with a focus on the greed for training labels.
ocar.resolution: They argue that substantial improvements of label and energy efficiency in machine learning may be required to address the challenge of acquiring the nanoscale connectome of a human brain.
ocar.future_work: Improvements of label and energy efficiency in machine learning are presented as required for a human nanoscale connectome; the abstract does not describe those methods.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope brain maps are huge, but the computers that trace them still need lots of hand-drawn labels. This review says that appetite for labels is a bottleneck, especially if the goal is a human brain map.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Motta, Schurr, Staffler, and Helmstaedter review big-data challenges in nanoscale connectomics. They argue that EM-based connectomics is especially hard by information content and analysis load, and that typical machine-learning practice still demands excessive labelled data while using only a small fraction of raw images. They frame label and energy efficiency as requirements for a human-brain nanoscale connectome.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No dataset sizes, label counts, or energy figures are given. “Gap between artificial and biological intelligence” is rhetorical, not a measured comparison.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope brain maps are huge, but the computers that trace them still need lots of hand-drawn labels. This review says that appetite for labels is a bottleneck, especially if the goal is a human brain map.

ocar.opportunity: Emerging connectomes of large circuits or entire nervous systems could guide theoretical models of neural computation and test their predictions.
ocar.challenge: There is not yet a standard set of tools for incorporating the connectivity constraints these datasets provide into the models typically studied in theoretical neuroscience.
ocar.action: Litwin-Kumar and Turaga, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), survey recent approaches to building models with constrained wiring diagrams and the insights they have provided.
ocar.resolution: The review catalogs existing methods and the insights they yielded, while arguing that new techniques are needed to scale these approaches to more complex datasets.
ocar.future_work: The authors describe challenges and the need for new techniques to scale constrained-wiring models to ever more complex datasets.

summaries.beginner: Wiring diagrams are arriving faster than theorists have standard tools to use them. This review surveys how people have put electron-microscope connections into computational models, and what is still missing.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Litwin-Kumar and Turaga survey how electron-microscopy wiring diagrams can constrain theoretical models of neural computation. They note there is not yet a standard set of tools for incorporating those constraints into typical theoretical-neuroscience models, review recent approaches and insights, and call for new techniques as datasets grow more complex.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not name specific models, organisms, or quantitative results. It is a survey, not a new algorithm paper.

plain_language_summary: Wiring diagrams are arriving faster than theorists have standard tools to use them. This review surveys how people have put electron-microscope connections into computational models, and what is still missing.

ocar.opportunity: Dense electron-microscopy reconstructions now map mammalian circuits at synaptic resolution, but function cannot be read from wiring unless synapse structure maps onto physiological strength.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether synapse size (postsynaptic-density area) relates to transmission strength (EPSP amplitude) in neocortex, and controversial how many release sites sit at a single synapse. Light-microscopic contact counts had supported a one-synapse, one-quantum view.
ocar.action: Holler, Köstinger, Martin, Schuhknecht, and Stratford, in Nature (2019), combined paired whole-cell recordings of synaptically connected pyramidal neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex slices with correlated light microscopy and high-resolution electron microscopy of all putative synaptic contacts between the recorded neurons.
ocar.resolution: They report a linear relationship between synapse size (PSD area) and strength (EPSP amplitude). Quantal analysis indicated that vesicle release sites exceed anatomical synapses by a factor of at least 2.7 in the abstract (at least 2.6 in the discussion), supporting multivesicular release. Synapses formed at only a fraction of light-microscopic appositions. Size–strength dependence was robust only when many responses were temporally averaged in stable slice recordings.
ocar.future_work: The exact structural basis of the release site remains unresolved; trans-synaptic nanocolumns, as described in hippocampus, are proposed as candidates testable with super-resolution methods on neocortical synapses. Independent regulation of release sites within a synapse is flagged as an open implication for computation.

summaries.beginner: How big a synapse looks under the electron microscope turns out to track how strongly it talks, at least in mouse cortex. The same work also suggests each synapse can dump more than one packet of transmitter at a time, which makes these contacts more flexible than a simple on/off switch.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2019), Holler, Köstinger, Martin, Schuhknecht, and Stratford paired slice electrophysiology of connected mouse somatosensory pyramidal cells with correlated light and high-resolution electron microscopy of all putative contacts. They report a linear relationship between postsynaptic-density area and EPSP amplitude, providing a basis for assigning physiological weights to EM-reconstructed synapses. Quantal analysis indicated at least about 2.6–2.7 release sites per anatomical synapse on average, challenging single-release-site models. Discussion notes that synapses form at only a fraction of light-microscopic appositions, so light-microscopic contact counts overestimate synapse number and underestimate presynaptic convergence.
summaries.advanced: The extract is a bioRxiv-formatted version of the Nature paper; how many connections or synapses were measured is not given here. The 2.6 versus 2.7 factor differs between discussion and abstract. Linearity of size versus strength is reported as robust only after temporal averaging in stable recordings, so single-trial EPSP amplitude is not claimed to read out PSD area. Multivesicular release is inferred from quantal analysis exceeding anatomical synapse counts, not from imaging vesicles in flight.

plain_language_summary: How big a synapse looks under the electron microscope turns out to track how strongly it talks, at least in mouse cortex. The same work also suggests each synapse can dump more than one packet of transmitter at a time, which makes these contacts more flexible than a simple on/off switch.

ocar.opportunity: The dense circuit structure of mammalian cerebral cortex is still unknown. Three-dimensional electron microscopy can image sizable neuropil, but dense reconstruction is the limiting step.
ocar.challenge: Prior dense cortical reconstructions were tiny (about 1,500 µm³) or sparse, and automated segmentation is too error-prone to be scientifically meaningful without efficient human–machine analysis.
ocar.action: Motta, Berning, Boergens, Staffler, Beining, Loomba, Schramm, Hennig, Wissler, and Helmstaedter, in Science (2018), report dense reconstruction of a volume of about 500,000 µm³ from layer 4 of mouse barrel cortex using a reconstruction technique they call FocusEM, investing about 4,000 human work hours.
ocar.resolution: They reconstructed about 0.9 m of dendrites and about 1.8 m of axons, about 300 times larger than previous dense mammalian cortical reconstructions and about 10–25 times more efficient. Connectomic data alone defined inhibitory axon types with subcellular target specificity; a fraction of excitatory axons also showed such specificity. Only about 35% of inhibitory and 55% of excitatory synaptic subcellular innervation was predicted from geometrical membrane availability, rejecting coarser random-wiring models for this layer-4 neuropil. They report enhanced variability of synaptic input composition at primary dendrites, evidence consistent with Hebbian weight adaptation in at least 24% of connections, and no such sign in at least 35%.
ocar.future_work: The authors present this as an approach to connectomic phenotyping of local dense mammalian cortex. The catalog abstract adds the possibility of screening across cortices, layers, species, developmental stages, sensory experience, and disease. The bioRxiv extract’s discussion was not captured (the selected text runs into the reference list).

summaries.beginner: Researchers densely traced a chunk of mouse whisker cortex hundreds of times larger than earlier complete maps. They find that who connects to whom is not just a matter of which wires happen to be nearby, and they look for traces of past learning in synapse sizes.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2018), Motta, Berning, Boergens, Staffler, and colleagues densely reconstructed about 500,000 µm³ of layer 4 mouse barrel cortex with FocusEM, about 300 times larger than prior dense mammalian cortical reconstructions, using about 4,000 human work hours for about 0.9 m of dendrites and 1.8 m of axons. They report that connectomic data alone can define inhibitory axon types with subcellular target specificity, that a fraction of excitatory axons show similar specificity, and that only about 35% of inhibitory and 55% of excitatory subcellular innervation is predicted from available membrane geometry. They also report evidence consistent with Hebbian weight adaptation in at least 24% of connections and no such sign in at least 35%.
summaries.advanced: The PDF extract is a bioRxiv preprint whose discussion was not captured (text jumps to the reference list). Efficiency “10–25 times” and the 24%/35% plasticity bounds are abstract claims without the supporting analyses in this extract. The catalog Science summary’s additional synapse censuses (for example 89 neurons; 153,171 synapses among neurites with at least 10 synapses) should be checked against the full paper. Rejecting coarser random-wiring models applies to subcellular innervation in this layer-4 volume, not to cortex generally.

plain_language_summary: Researchers densely traced a chunk of mouse whisker cortex hundreds of times larger than earlier complete maps. They find that who connects to whom is not just a matter of which wires happen to be nearby, and they look for traces of past learning in synapse sizes.

ocar.opportunity: A complete Drosophila connectome could support causal tests of behaviour by silencing or activating identified circuits, and could reveal unsuspected pathways, much as genomics did for molecular biology.
ocar.challenge: Human proofreading of segmented bodies remains the most time-consuming step. Major versus minor pathways need to be distinguished, and vertebrate brains and cognitive disorders remain distant applications.
ocar.action: Meinertzhagen, in Journal of Experimental Biology (2018), offers a personal perspective on the Drosophila connectome, covering focused ion beam–scanning electron microscopy, reconstruction progress in fly brain regions, and what a complete map would enable.
ocar.resolution: He notes large progress in Drosophila synaptic circuits; useful distinctions include major pathways (100 or more presynaptic contacts) versus minor ones (fewer than about 10); most neurites are both pre- and postsynaptic; and all synaptic sites have multiple postsynaptic dendrites. Complete adult and larval connectomes are described as imminent. Value is causal behaviour via cell-specific transgenes plus discovery of unexpected pathways and evolutionary comparison.
ocar.future_work: Circuit information will be required to understand how differences between brains underlie differences in behaviour, to herald more advanced connectomic strategies for the vertebrate brain, and eventually to understand cognitive disorders with a connectomic basis.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly brains are small enough that a complete wiring diagram is becoming realistic. This essay argues that such a map will let researchers turn circuits on and off to explain behaviour, and will turn up pathways nobody expected.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Experimental Biology (2018), Meinertzhagen reviews Drosophila connectomics enabled by FIB-SEM, image alignment, and computer-aided reconstruction. He distinguishes major pathways (100 or more presynaptic contacts) from minor ones (fewer than about 10), notes that most neurites are both pre- and postsynaptic, and that synaptic sites are polyadic. He expects a complete adult fly connectome within a few years and a larval one possibly sooner, with human proofreading as the remaining bottleneck. He argues the map will support causal behavioural tests via cell-specific transgenes and will reveal unsuspected pathways.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Timeline claims (“next few years”) are 2018 predictions, not results. No quantitative reconstruction completeness is given. The piece is a perspective, not a new dataset.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly brains are small enough that a complete wiring diagram is becoming realistic. This essay argues that such a map will let researchers turn circuits on and off to explain behaviour, and will turn up pathways nobody expected.

ocar.opportunity: Teravoxel volume electron-microscopy datasets from neural tissue can now be acquired in weeks, but analysis still takes years of manual labor.
ocar.challenge: Inferring a richly annotated synaptic connectivity matrix from reconstructions is labor-limited.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald, Schubert, Killinger, Urban, Mikula, Svara, and Kornfeld, in Nature Methods (2017), developed the SyConn framework, which uses deep convolutional neural networks and random forest classifiers to infer an annotated connectivity matrix from manual neurite skeleton reconstructions.
ocar.resolution: SyConn automatically identifies mitochondria, synapses and their types, axons, dendrites, spines, myelin, somata, and cell types. The authors tested the approach on serial block-face electron-microscopy datasets from zebrafish, mouse, and zebra finch, and computed the synaptic wiring of songbird basal ganglia. They found, for example, that basal-ganglia cell types with high firing rates in vivo had higher densities of mitochondria and vesicles, and that synapse sizes and quantities scaled systematically with the innervated postsynaptic cell types.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not state further work; implied use is replacing years of manual annotation with automatic inference on new volumes.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope stacks of brain tissue are now collected much faster than people can label them. This team trains computers to mark synapses, cell parts, and cell types on already-traced neurons, then uses that to study songbird wiring.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2017), Dorkenwald and colleagues present SyConn, which uses deep convolutional nets and random forests to infer an annotated synaptic connectivity matrix from manual neurite skeletons, automatically identifying mitochondria, synapses and their types, axons, dendrites, spines, myelin, somata, and cell types. They tested the approach on serial block-face EM from zebrafish, mouse, and zebra finch and computed synaptic wiring of songbird basal ganglia. They report that basal-ganglia cell types with high in vivo firing rates had higher mitochondria and vesicle densities, and that synapse sizes and quantities scaled with postsynaptic cell type.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No accuracy metrics, dataset sizes, or firing-rate statistics are given. “High firing rates in vivo” is a qualitative example, not a reported number.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope stacks of brain tissue are now collected much faster than people can label them. This team trains computers to mark synapses, cell parts, and cell types on already-traced neurons, then uses that to study songbird wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Parallels with vertebrates plus Drosophila genetic tools make the fly a powerful system for mechanistic behaviour. Large light-microscopy resources combined with 3D electron microscopy can characterize neuron types at scale.
ocar.challenge: An adult whole-brain electron-microscopy dataset is about 40 times larger than the larva and would require about 500–5,000 person-years of manual labour. Light and electron microscopy outputs must also be integrated with physiology.
ocar.action: Schlegel, Costa, and Jefferis, in Current Opinion in Insect Science (2017), review available Drosophila data and tools, the approaching larval whole-brain connectome, the public adult whole-brain electron-microscopy dataset, and prospects for larger insects and vertebrates.
ocar.resolution: They report a larval whole-brain connectome approaching completion by manual reconstruction, an adult whole-brain dataset already public with focused reconstruction underway, and they expect rapid improvements in imaging and automated segmentation to deliver a complete adult connectome in the next five years (from 2017). They argue that light and electron microscopy must be integrated with functional data into comprehensive databases.
ocar.future_work: They consider limits and potential of future progress and how this may impact neuroscience in larger insects and vertebrates. Integration of light microscopy, electron microscopy, and physiology into databases is required.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly genetics and new 3D maps are making it realistic to list every neuron and many of its connections. This review says the larva is nearly done by hand, the adult volume is public, and automated tracing will have to finish the adult brain.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Insect Science (2017), Schlegel, Costa, and Jefferis review Drosophila resources: large light-microscopy datasets, driver lines, activity tools, and 3D electron microscopy. They state a whole-brain larval connectome is approaching completion by manual reconstruction, while an adult whole-brain dataset is already public but its 40× greater volume would require about 500–5,000 person-years of manual labour. They predict automated segmentation will likely deliver a complete adult connectome within five years and argue that light and electron microscopy must be integrated with functional data.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The 500–5,000 person-year and five-year adult-connectome figures are 2017 estimates, not measurements. No new reconstructions are presented.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly genetics and new 3D maps are making it realistic to list every neuron and many of its connections. This review says the larva is nearly done by hand, the adult volume is public, and automated tracing will have to finish the adult brain.

ocar.opportunity: Neurite reconstruction speed limits which connectomes can realistically be mapped. Faster in-browser annotation could extend that range.
ocar.challenge: Existing annotation tools are too slow for three-dimensional electron-microscopic data from mammalian cortex.
ocar.action: Boergens, Berning, Bocklisch, Bräunlein, Drawitsch, Frohnhofen, Herold, Otto, Rzepka, Werkmeister, Werner, Wiese, Wissler, and Helmstaedter, in Nature Methods (2017), report webKnossos, an in-browser annotation tool with flight mode, a single-view egocentric reconstruction method for trained annotator crowds.
ocar.resolution: Trained crowds reconstructed at 1.5 ± 0.6 mm/h for axons and 2.1 ± 0.9 mm/h for dendrites in 3D electron-microscopic data from mammalian cortex. webKnossos accelerated neurite reconstruction 4- to 13-fold compared with then-current state-of-the-art tools.
ocar.future_work: The abstract states this extends the range of connectomes that can realistically be mapped; it does not detail further experiments.

summaries.beginner: Tracing neurons through 3D microscope stacks is slow. This browser tool lets trained people “fly” along axons and dendrites several times faster than previous software, which matters when the maps get huge.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2017), Boergens, Berning, and colleagues present webKnossos, an in-browser 3D electron-microscopy annotation tool whose flight mode is a single-view egocentric reconstruction method. They report trained annotator crowds reconstructing at 1.5 ± 0.6 mm/h for axons and 2.1 ± 0.9 mm/h for dendrites in mammalian cortex, a 4- to 13-fold speedup versus then-current tools.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The comparison tools are not named, nor are dataset identity, number of annotators, or error rates. Speed is reported as 1.5 ± 0.6 and 2.1 ± 0.9 mm/h without stating whether the uncertainty is a standard deviation.

plain_language_summary: Tracing neurons through 3D microscope stacks is slow. This browser tool lets trained people “fly” along axons and dendrites several times faster than previous software, which matters when the maps get huge.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy has made data acquisition feasible for circuits comprising a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, bringing comprehensive mapping of densely packed neuronal networks closer.
ocar.challenge: Data analysis is massively lagging behind imaging for cellular-resolution connectomics.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, in Nature Methods (2013), summarizes and quantifies the challenges for data analysis in cellular-resolution connectomics and describes then-current solutions involving online crowdsourcing and machine-learning approaches.
ocar.resolution: The perspective frames analysis—not acquisition—as the bottleneck for circuits of a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, and points to crowdsourcing and machine learning as current responses.
ocar.future_work: The implied need is to close the analysis lag with better crowdsourcing and machine-learning pipelines.

summaries.beginner: Taking three-dimensional microscope pictures of circuits is getting easier; turning those pictures into wiring diagrams is not. This 2013 perspective tallies why analysis is the bottleneck and how crowds and machine learning were starting to help.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2013), Helmstaedter argues that neuronal networks are high-dimensional graphs packed at extreme density, so comprehensive mapping is a major challenge. He states that volume electron microscopy has made acquisition feasible for circuits of a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, but that data analysis is massively lagging. The perspective summarizes analysis challenges and describes then-current online crowdsourcing and machine-learning solutions.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No quantitative analysis rates are actually given in the abstract despite the “quantify” claim. It is a 2013 perspective, not a methods benchmark.

plain_language_summary: Taking three-dimensional microscope pictures of circuits is getting easier; turning those pictures into wiring diagrams is not. This 2013 perspective tallies why analysis is the bottleneck and how crowds and machine learning were starting to help.

ocar.opportunity: Invertebrate circuits whose connectivities are known can teach what information beyond a wiring diagram is needed to understand function, with lessons for large vertebrate circuits.
ocar.challenge: Neuronal dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits mean a connectome underdetermines function.
ocar.action: Bargmann and Marder, in Nature Methods (2013), ask in a Historical Perspective what information is needed beyond connectivity diagrams, informed by invertebrate circuits with known wiring, and compare those features to the vertebrate retina.
ocar.resolution: They highlight neuronal dynamics and neuromodulation and the existence of parallel circuits. Vertebrate retina shares these features, suggesting generality across animals. They suggest approaches to study the functional organization of large circuits based on existing knowledge of small circuits.
ocar.future_work: Comparisons across these systems suggest approaches to study large circuits based on knowledge of small circuits; the abstract does not enumerate a methods list.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram is not a user manual. This essay uses well-mapped small nervous systems to argue that timing, chemical modulation, and backup pathways are also needed to explain what a circuit does.
summaries.intermediate: In a Nature Methods (2013) Historical Perspective, Bargmann and Marder ask what is needed beyond connectivity to understand nervous-system function. Drawing on invertebrate circuits with known wiring, they emphasize neuronal dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits. They note that vertebrate retina shares these features, suggesting generality, and they sketch how knowledge of small circuits can guide study of large ones.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No new data, species list, or quantitative claims are provided. The piece is conceptual.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram is not a user manual. This essay uses well-mapped small nervous systems to argue that timing, chemical modulation, and backup pathways are also needed to explain what a circuit does.

ocar.opportunity: Most model organisms lack high-resolution maps of early visual circuitry. The microinsect Megaphragma viggianii, small yet behaviourally non-trivial, offers a tractable whole-organism connectomics target.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing a complete early visual system in an adult insect is still rare, which limits computational models of insect vision.
ocar.action: Chua, Gunn, Villani, Cohen, Thasin, Wu, Shefter, Pang, Xu, Makarova, Hess, Polilov, Chklovskii, and colleagues, in Current Biology (2023), image the whole head of Megaphragma viggianii with serial electron microscopy, reconstruct the compound eye, analyze ommatidial optics, and reconstruct the lamina connectome.
ocar.resolution: Compared with the fruit fly and the honeybee, the Megaphragma visual system is highly simplified: 29 ommatidia per eye and six lamina neuron types. The authors report features that are both stereotypical among most ommatidia and specialized to some. They present these as “barebones” circuits critical for flying insects, intended to facilitate computational models of insect visual processing.
ocar.future_work: The results are framed as facilitating computational models of visual processing in insects; the abstract does not report those models.

summaries.beginner: A very small flying insect has a stripped-down eye: 29 little lenses and six kinds of first-hop visual neurons. Mapping that simple circuit is meant to show the minimum wiring a flying insect needs to see.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2023), Chua and colleagues image the whole head of the microinsect Megaphragma viggianii with serial electron microscopy, reconstruct the compound eye, analyze ommatidial optics, and reconstruct the lamina connectome. They report 29 ommatidia per eye and six lamina neuron types, a simplification relative to fruit fly and honeybee, with both stereotypical and ommatidium-specialized features. They argue these “barebones” circuits can support computational models of insect visual processing.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Catalog author metadata are truncated and duplicated. The abstract does not give synapse counts, completeness metrics, or optical measurements. Comparison to fly and bee is qualitative.

plain_language_summary: A very small flying insect has a stripped-down eye: 29 little lenses and six kinds of first-hop visual neurons. Mapping that simple circuit is meant to show the minimum wiring a flying insect needs to see.

ocar.opportunity: Defining organizational principles of neuronal networks at the cellular scale, or micro-connectomics, is a key challenge. Graph-theoretical parameters, often informed by Ramón y Cajal’s conservation laws, offer a language for that.
ocar.challenge: It remains to evaluate whether cellular networks reflect an economical trade-off between biological cost and functional value.
ocar.action: Schröter, Paulsen, and Bullmore, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2017), review graph-theoretical parameters of micro-connectome topology from intact small organisms and from samples of larger nervous systems, then evaluate evidence for an economical cost–value trade-off.
ocar.resolution: Various results suggest that many aspects of neuronal network organization are the outcome of competition between biological cost and functional value.
ocar.future_work: The review frames this trade-off as an organizing principle to test further; the abstract does not list specific open experiments.

summaries.beginner: Small wiring diagrams can be scored like maps: how clustered, how long the wires, how expensive. This review argues that many cellular networks look like a compromise between saving biological cost and keeping useful function.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2017), Schröter, Paulsen, and Bullmore review micro-connectomics—organization of neuronal networks at cellular scale—using graph-theoretical parameters often motivated by Ramón y Cajal’s conservation laws. They summarize results from intact small organisms and from samples of larger nervous systems, then evaluate evidence for an economical trade-off between biological cost and functional value. They conclude that many aspects of network organization appear to result from competition between those pressures.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No specific graph metrics, species, or statistical tests are named. “Economical trade-off” is a synthesis claim, not a new measurement.

plain_language_summary: Small wiring diagrams can be scored like maps: how clustered, how long the wires, how expensive. This review argues that many cellular networks look like a compromise between saving biological cost and keeping useful function.

ocar.opportunity: Reconstructing neuronal connectivity from streaming electron microscopy requires automated pixel-level segmentation at the pace of multi-beam microscopes, near a terabyte per hour.
ocar.challenge: Existing algorithms provide relatively good accuracy but are unacceptably slow and would require years to extract connectivity graphs from even a single cubic millimetre of neural tissue.
ocar.action: Meirovitch, Matveev, Saribekyan, Budden, Rolnick, Ódor, Knowles-Barley, Jones, Pfister, Lichtman, and Shavit, on arXiv (2016), present a multi-pass pipeline optimized for shared-memory multicore systems: an initial fast-pass followed by a slow-pass that iteratively corrects errors, using shallow convolutional nets, parallel watershed, and object merging.
ocar.resolution: They reconstruct the full Kasthuri et al. dataset (abstract: 463 GB capturing 120,000 cubic microns) from image stack to skeletons in hours on a single multicore machine rather than weeks on larger distributed systems. Conclusions report 6 nm execution in 5 hours on the entire S1 dataset with variation of information 1.83 on AC3-256 (trained on AC4-100); 3 nm improved VI to 1.66. A prior speed-benchmarked pipeline took 3 weeks with VI 1.99, versus 1.77 when their pipeline was evaluated on the same test portion. They also present slow-pass X-junction detection and a MaskExtend CNN (validation accuracy nearly 95% after 100K training iterations).
ocar.future_work: They suggest new methods for detecting morphological errors and present the slow-pass as a framework for error detection and correction. Conclusions emphasize time-constrained connectomics as a complement to systems that optimize for accuracy alone.

summaries.beginner: Brain electron-microscope movies arrive faster than old tracing software can keep up. This pipeline does a quick first pass on one powerful computer, then a slower cleanup pass, and it finishes a classic cubic-chunk dataset in hours instead of weeks.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on arXiv (2016), Meirovitch, Matveev, and colleagues describe a multi-pass connectomics pipeline for shared-memory multicore machines, aimed at near terabyte-per-hour multi-beam electron-microscope rates. A fast-pass (shallow convolutional nets, parallel watershed, agglomeration) is followed by a slow-pass for morphological error detection, including X-junctions, and MaskExtend. They report reconstructing the full Kasthuri S1 volume (abstract: 463 GB, 120,000 µm³) to skeletons in hours on one machine. On AC3-256 they report variation-of-information 1.83 at 6 nm (5 hours for S1) and 1.66 at 3 nm, versus a prior speed-benchmarked pipeline at VI 1.99 after 3 weeks (1.77 on the same test portion for their method).
summaries.advanced: Volume and byte-size figures disagree slightly between abstract (463 GB, 120,000 µm³) and conclusions (about 473 GB, about 100,000 µm³). VI scores are on named test sets (AC3-256), not a claim of biological proofreading quality. “Nearly 95%” is validation accuracy of a mask CNN after 100K iterations, not connectome accuracy. The extract does not report synapse detection performance. This is an arXiv methods preprint.

plain_language_summary: Brain electron-microscope movies arrive faster than old tracing software can keep up. This pipeline does a quick first pass on one powerful computer, then a slower cleanup pass, and it finishes a classic cubic-chunk dataset in hours instead of weeks.

ocar.opportunity: Knowing the fly central-nervous-system connectome is crucial to understanding behaviour. Several laboratories, especially Janelia, have initiated this effort, farthest along in optic neuropils.
ocar.challenge: Light-microscopic candidate partners are not reliable synaptic partners. Degeneracy in pathway elements can foil cell-by-cell causal tests.
ocar.action: Meinertzhagen, in Journal of Neurogenetics (2016), offers a short perspective on Drosophila connectome studies, distinguishing electron microscopy (especially focused-ion beam milling scanning electron microscopy) from light-microscopic proximity methods, and relating fly work to C. elegans and the vertebrate retina.
ocar.resolution: Ultrastructural synaptic partnerships provide a heuristic to interpret and predict functional interactions, often revealing unexpected pathways. Circuit analysis may proceed cell by cell (interrupt or restore function) but can be foiled by degeneracy; circuit motifs and higher-order network properties are another use. These attempts anticipate parallel work on the vertebrate inner plexiform layer and augment the C. elegans connectome.
ocar.future_work: Parallel attempts in other systems, notably the inner plexiform layer of the vertebrate retina, and use of circuit information to analyse motifs and higher-order network properties.

summaries.beginner: Seeing two fly neurons sit near each other is not the same as knowing they synapse. This perspective argues that electron-microscope synapses, not light-microscope proximity, are what let us guess and test how fly circuits work.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neurogenetics (2016), Meinertzhagen reviews Drosophila connectome efforts, especially at Janelia and in optic neuropils, using electron microscopy (particularly FIB-SEM) as distinct from light-microscopic maps of genetically labelled cell types. He argues that proximity only yields candidate partners and that ultrastructure often reveals unexpected pathways. He notes that cell-by-cell causal tests can be foiled by degeneracy, and that circuit motifs and higher-order network properties are additional uses. He places the work alongside the C. elegans connectome and anticipated retina inner-plexiform reconstructions.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No new electron-microscopy volumes or completeness numbers are given. It is a perspective.

plain_language_summary: Seeing two fly neurons sit near each other is not the same as knowing they synapse. This perspective argues that electron-microscope synapses, not light-microscope proximity, are what let us guess and test how fly circuits work.

ocar.opportunity: A structure–function model linking mind, brain, and behavior needs a connectome: a complete matrix of structural connections between the nodes of a nervous system, described at nested scales.
ocar.challenge: The greatest challenge today is extracting knowledge and understanding of nervous-system structure–function architecture from vast amounts of data. A connectome is necessary but not sufficient.
ocar.action: Swanson and Lichtman, in Annual Review of Neuroscience (2016), review the history of systems-level nervous-system maps from fifth-century macrolevel attempts through Cajal at meso- and microlevels to mid-twentieth-century electron microscopy at the nanolevel.
ocar.resolution: They define four nested levels of connection: macroconnections between gray-matter regions, mesoconnections between neuron types, microconnections between individual neurons, and nanoconnections at synapses. A connectome is framed as a necessary but not sufficient foundation for a structure–function model.
ocar.future_work: Extracting knowledge and understanding of structure–function architecture from vast amounts of data is identified as the greatest present challenge.

summaries.beginner: A full list of brain connections would help, but it would not by itself explain mind and behaviour. This historical review sorts connections into four nested scales, from brain regions down to synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Neuroscience (2016), Swanson and Lichtman survey attempts to understand the nervous system as a system, from fifth-century macrolevel maps through Cajal in the late nineteenth century to electron microscopy at the nanolevel in the mid-twentieth century. They define a connectome as a complete matrix of structural connections, necessary but not sufficient for a structure–function model, and distinguish macro-, meso-, micro-, and nanoconnections. They identify extracting understanding from vast data as the present challenge.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No datasets or quantitative results are given. “Fifth century” origin of macrolevel attempts is the authors’ historical framing.

plain_language_summary: A full list of brain connections would help, but it would not by itself explain mind and behaviour. This historical review sorts connections into four nested scales, from brain regions down to synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Cellular-resolution connectomics needs scalable image-analysis algorithms that require minimal user intervention. Deep learning has transformed image classification and is promising for electron-microscopy segmentation.
ocar.challenge: U-net-style architectures still leave room to deepen residual networks and improve accuracy on densely packed neuronal membranes and related structures.
ocar.action: Quan, Hildebrand, and Jeong introduce FusionNet in Frontiers in Computer Science (2021; arXiv 2016): a deep fully residual convolutional network that combines semantic segmentation, residual networks, and summation-based skip connections for automatic segmentation of neuronal structures.
ocar.resolution: They report improved segmentation accuracy versus several popular electron-microscopy methods, demonstrated on cell-membrane and cell-nucleus tasks. FusionNetW416 outperformed U-net and RDN on foreground-restricted Rand and information-theoretic scores after border thinning and on the Dice coefficient. They deployed the trained network to 16,000 sections of larval zebrafish brain at 56.4 × 56.4 × ~60 nm³, about 1.2 terabytes.
ocar.future_work: Approaches that improve the prediction accuracy of such deep networks are flagged as an important goal for future work.

summaries.beginner: Computers still struggle to outline every neuron in electron-microscope pictures. This network, FusionNet, stacks extra residual shortcuts and is shown tracing membranes and cell nuclei, including on a large larval zebrafish brain volume.
summaries.intermediate: Quan, Hildebrand, and Jeong present FusionNet (arXiv 2016; Frontiers in Computer Science 2021), a fully residual convolutional net that uses summation-based skip connections to deepen U-net-style architectures for connectomics electron microscopy. They compare it with other popular EM segmentation methods and show membrane and nucleus tasks. In the extract, FusionNetW416 scores higher than U-net and RDN on foreground-restricted Rand and information-theoretic scores after border thinning and on Dice. They apply the trained net to 16,000 sections of larval zebrafish brain (about 1.2 TB) at 56.4 × 56.4 × ~60 nm³.
summaries.advanced: Table 3’s numeric metric values are not reproduced in the extract, only the ranking versus U-net and RDN. Catalog year is 2016 (preprint) while the journal version is 2021. Flexibility is illustrated on two tasks, not a full synaptic connectome. Future-work text on improving deep-network accuracy is generic. Competing methods beyond U-net and RDN are not fully named in the captured text.

plain_language_summary: Computers still struggle to outline every neuron in electron-microscope pictures. This network, FusionNet, stacks extra residual shortcuts and is shown tracing membranes and cell nuclei, including on a large larval zebrafish brain volume.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic segmentations of nanometer-scale electron-microscopy volumes still require many manual corrections. Humans can split, merge, and adjust segments, so better interactive tools could cut that cost.
ocar.challenge: Proofreading is time-consuming. Tool design for accuracy, speed, and usability is under-evaluated, and automatic algorithms require hundreds of corrections per cubic micron of tissue.
ocar.action: Haehn, Knowles-Barley, Roberts, Beyer, Kasthuri, Lichtman, and Pfister, in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2014), present Mojo, a fully featured single-user desktop proofreading application, and Dojo, a multi-user web application, and evaluate them against Raveler (Janelia Farm) in a between-subjects user study with non-experts on a public connectomics dataset.
ocar.resolution: Web-based Dojo showed a significant improvement of corrections given the same amount of time, and all participants using Dojo reported better usability. The authors discuss findings and provide an analysis of requirements for designing visual proofreading software.
ocar.future_work: They provide an analysis of requirements for designing visual proofreading software; the abstract does not list those requirements.

summaries.beginner: Automatic maps of neurons are full of small mistakes that people have to fix. This paper builds two proofreading programs and finds that a web tool lets non-experts correct more in a fixed time than the alternatives they tested.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2014), Haehn and colleagues present Mojo, a single-user desktop proofreading app, and Dojo, a multi-user web app, for correcting automatic segmentations of nanometer-scale electron microscopy. They ran a between-subjects study asking non-experts to proofread neurons in a public connectomics dataset, comparing Mojo, Dojo, and Janelia’s Raveler. They report significantly more corrections with Dojo in the same time and better usability ratings from all Dojo participants.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not name the dataset, number of participants, or effect sizes. “Hundreds of corrections per cubic micron” is given as background, not a result of this study.

plain_language_summary: Automatic maps of neurons are full of small mistakes that people have to fix. This paper builds two proofreading programs and finds that a web tool lets non-experts correct more in a fixed time than the alternatives they tested.

ocar.opportunity: Reconstructions of small but biologically interesting circuits have already yielded functional insights. Scaling to larger circuits, and eventually whole animals, is the next need.
ocar.challenge: Those reconstructions were heroic proof-of-concept experiments, requiring person-months of effort per neuron, and will not scale.
ocar.action: Plaza, Scheffer, and Chklovskii, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2014), examine what will be required to generate and use substantially larger connectomes, listing five areas that need increased attention.
ocar.resolution: The five areas are: imaging better suited to automatic reconstruction, with excellent z-resolution; automatic detection, validation, and measurement of synapses; reconstruction methods that keep and use uncertainty metrics for every object from initial images through connectome queries; processes that are fully incremental so the connectome may be used before it is complete; and better tools for analysis of connectomes once they are obtained.
ocar.future_work: Those five areas are the agenda the authors set; the abstract does not add further experiments.

summaries.beginner: A few small wiring diagrams exist, but they took enormous effort per cell. This review lists five upgrades—better 3D images, automatic synapses, tracking uncertainty, using incomplete maps, and better analysis tools—needed before much larger brains can be reconstructed.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2014), Plaza, Scheffer, and Chklovskii argue that existing connectome reconstructions were proof-of-concept efforts requiring person-months per neuron and will not scale. They list five needs: imaging suited to automatic reconstruction with excellent z-resolution; automatic synapse detection, validation, and measurement; uncertainty-aware reconstruction from pixels through queries; incremental use of incomplete connectomes; and better analysis tools.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No new data or timings beyond “person-months per neuron” are given. It is a requirements survey.

plain_language_summary: A few small wiring diagrams exist, but they took enormous effort per cell. This review lists five upgrades—better 3D images, automatic synapses, tracking uncertainty, using incomplete maps, and better analysis tools—needed before much larger brains can be reconstructed.

ocar.opportunity: Electron-microscopy volumes hundreds of terabytes in size are segmented with a diverse, multi-user tool set. Tracking the state, progress, and evolution of that work is itself a problem connectomics needs to solve.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation of a single volume is complex, time-intensive, and split across many tools and users. Provenance, accountability, and auditing are lacking.
ocar.action: Al-Awami, Beyer, Haehn, Kasthuri, Lichtman, Pfister, and Hadwiger, in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2016), present NeuroBlocks, a multi-user web visualization system that integrates manual and semi-automatic segmentation, proofreading, visualization, and analysis tools.
ocar.resolution: They describe NeuroBlocks as the first system integrating this heterogeneous tool set for management, provenance, accountability, and auditing of large-scale segmentations. Utility is demonstrated in two case studies focused on different user roles in a large real-world connectomics project.
ocar.future_work: Implied continued use is tracking segmentation and proofreading progress in large projects; the abstract does not list further technical extensions.

summaries.beginner: Huge brain-map projects use many programs and many people, so it is easy to lose track of what has been proofread. NeuroBlocks is a web dashboard meant to show the state and history of that work.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2016), Al-Awami and colleagues present NeuroBlocks, a multi-user web application for tracking the state, progress, and evolution of very large volumetric segmentation in neuroscience. It is designed to integrate the diverse tools used for manual and semi-automatic segmentation, proofreading, visualization, and analysis, providing management, provenance, accountability, and auditing. They demonstrate the design with two case studies of different user roles in a large real-world connectomics project.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not name the project, volume size beyond “hundreds of terabytes” as field background, or quantitative user-study outcomes. “First system” is an authorship claim.

plain_language_summary: Huge brain-map projects use many programs and many people, so it is easy to lose track of what has been proofread. NeuroBlocks is a web dashboard meant to show the state and history of that work.

ocar.opportunity: Dense electron-microscopy connectomes now visualize every cell type, neuron, and synapse along the Drosophila early olfactory pathway, a leading model of olfactory processing and associative memory.
ocar.challenge: A wiring diagram does not by itself reveal functional logic. The feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback of large-scale multi-input multi-output neurons, and a quantitative account also needs a model of natural odorants and real-time causality.
ocar.action: Lazar and Zhou, on arXiv (2026), review early-olfactory-system connectome and synaptome datasets of the past fifteen years and argue that feedback-loop abstractions, odorant-object semantics and syntax, and causal stage-by-stage cascades are the foundation of functional logic.
ocar.resolution: They conclude that local processing at each neuropil stage is carried out by dense feedback around multi-input multi-output neurons, that computational models of those loops are necessary because such neurons are hard to probe experimentally, that odorant objects define semantics and syntax and call for new distance measures for associative memory, and that circuits must be treated as real-time cascades of giant local feedback loops. They note that the same architecture recurs in fly vision (medulla and lobula plate).
ocar.future_work: Quantitative understanding requires models that hold feedback, input-space structure, and causal cascade together. Open questions include whether mushroom-body compartment circuits distinguish odorant semantics, how much computational power and memory capacity they offer, and testing associative-learning models with timing codes such as marked first-spike sequences. Results may inform olfaction in other animals, including primates and humans, where connectomes remain difficult.

summaries.beginner: Having a complete wiring diagram of the fruit fly’s early smell pathway is not the same as knowing how it computes. This review says you also need the local feedback loops, a model of real-world odors, and respect for the fact that each stage runs in real time.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on arXiv (2026), Lazar and Zhou review Drosophila early-olfactory connectome and synaptome data from the past fifteen years. They argue that the textbook feedforward antenna-to-mushroom-body pathway is embedded in dense local feedback of large-scale multi-input multi-output neurons, and that feedback-loop abstractions are the foundation of the circuit’s functional logic. They further argue that a quantitative account needs an explicit model of odorant objects (semantics and syntax) and must treat the pathway as a causal, real-time cascade. Conclusions extend the same need to other fly sensory systems such as medulla and lobula plate.
summaries.advanced: This is a review and perspective, not a new reconstruction or physiology dataset. Claims about multi-input multi-output feedback and odorant objects are interpretive. The extract does not quantify synapse counts or loop gains. Catalog journal metadata are empty; venue is arXiv (2026). Experimental inaccessibility of high-fan-in and high-fan-out neurons is asserted, not demonstrated here.

plain_language_summary: Having a complete wiring diagram of the fruit fly’s early smell pathway is not the same as knowing how it computes. This review says you also need the local feedback loops, a model of real-world odors, and respect for the fact that each stage runs in real time.

ocar.opportunity: Combining a synapse-level connectome with developmental cell-adhesion-molecule expression and binding specificities could identify receptor–ligand pairs that match neurons to synaptic targets.
ocar.challenge: Developing neurons encounter many axons and dendrites but synapse with only a subset. Identifying receptor–ligand pairs that directly match partners has been hard amid the diversity of cell-adhesion molecules.
ocar.action: Yoo, Dombrovski, Mirshahidi, Nern, LoCascio, Zipursky, and Kurmangaliyev, in Current Biology (2023), integrated the Drosophila visual motion-detection connectome with developmental expression patterns and binding specificities of cell-adhesion molecules, focusing on closely related T4/T5 subtypes that choose alternative synaptic targets in adjacent neuropil layers.
ocar.resolution: Layer choice correlates with matching expression of Beat and Side family receptor–ligand pairs in synaptic partners. Genetic analysis showed that presynaptic Side-II and postsynaptic Beat-VI restrict synaptic partners to the same layer; removing the pair disrupts layers and leads to inappropriate targeting of presynaptic sites and postsynaptic dendrites. The authors propose that different Side/Beat pairs collaborate with other recognition molecules to determine wiring specificities.
ocar.future_work: They propose that combining transcriptomes, connectomes, and protein-interactome maps allows unbiased identification of brain-wiring determinants more broadly, in collaboration with other recognition molecules.

summaries.beginner: Closely related fly motion-sensing cells pick different layers to wire into. This study finds matching pairs of sticky surface proteins that keep partners in the same layer; taking one pair away scrambles the layers.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2023), Yoo and colleagues integrate a synapse-level Drosophila visual-system connectome with developmental cell-adhesion-molecule expression and binding specificities. Focusing on related T4/T5 subtypes that choose alternative synaptic targets in adjacent layers, they report matching Beat/Side receptor–ligand pairs in partners. Genetics showed presynaptic Side-II and postsynaptic Beat-VI restrict partners to the same layer; removing the pair disrupts layers and mis-targets presynaptic sites and postsynaptic dendrites.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No cell counts, statistical tests, or expression-timing details are given. The claim that combining omics maps allows unbiased identification of wiring determinants is a concluding proposal, not a genome-wide screen result reported here.

plain_language_summary: Closely related fly motion-sensing cells pick different layers to wire into. This study finds matching pairs of sticky surface proteins that keep partners in the same layer; taking one pair away scrambles the layers.

ocar.opportunity: A near-term Drosophila melanogaster connectome (roughly 200,000 neurons), together with behavioural richness and genetic tools, makes the fly brain an enticing complete-system target.
ocar.challenge: A connectome alone is not enough to understand the brain. Additional data must be obtained, collated, and organized for an integrated model.
ocar.action: Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, in Journal of Experimental Biology (2021), itemize the data still needed—beyond an imminent electron-microscopy-level description of all neurons and chemical synapses—to build an integrated model of the D. melanogaster brain.
ocar.resolution: They argue that within a few years a connectome will exist, and they collate what more must be gathered for an integrated brain model. The catalog abstract does not enumerate the punch-list items themselves.
ocar.future_work: The paper’s purpose is the list of still-needed data; the abstract does not enumerate it, so those items cannot be restated here.

summaries.beginner: A complete fruit-fly wiring diagram is coming, but the authors say that map by itself will not explain the fly’s brain. Their essay asks what extra measurements still have to be gathered and organized.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Experimental Biology (2021), Scheffer and Meinertzhagen note that Drosophila melanogaster (roughly 200,000 neurons) is a near-term whole-brain connectome target given behavioural richness and genetic tools. They take as given that an electron-microscopy-level description of all neurons and chemical synapses will soon exist, and they ask what more is needed for an integrated brain model, itemizing data to obtain, collate, and organize.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not actually list the missing data types, so this card cannot enumerate them without inventing content. Neuron count “roughly 200,000” is the authors’ 2021 figure.

plain_language_summary: A complete fruit-fly wiring diagram is coming, but the authors say that map by itself will not explain the fly’s brain. Their essay asks what extra measurements still have to be gathered and organized.

ocar.opportunity: Inhibitory cortical circuits have distinctive synaptic target preference, but a comprehensive map of how that preference develops postnatally has been missing. High-throughput three-dimensional electron microscopy now allows repeated connectomic experiments across developmental time points.
ocar.challenge: The time course of interneuron integration is only beginning to be understood, and a systematic mapping of cortical inhibitory innervation during postnatal development was lacking.
ocar.action: Gour, Boergens, Heike, Hua, Laserstein, Song, and Helmstaedter, in Science (2020), mapped connectivity in 13 three-dimensional electron-microscopy datasets from layers 4 and 2/3 of mouse primary somatosensory cortex at postnatal days 5, 7, 9, 14, 28, and 56, focusing on inhibitory innervation of cell bodies, apical dendrites, and axon initial segments.
ocar.resolution: Apical-dendrite-preferring axons already show high target preference at early time points (almost adult levels at P5). Soma innervation is established gradually, with a peak of change between P7 and P9 (preference increased almost threefold; synapse density along those axons dropped almost twofold), consistent with removal of misplaced synapses. Axo-axonic innervation starts as a minor fraction and develops to provide about 50% of synaptic input to the axon initial segment; chandelier axons show first target preference by P14 and develop full specificity almost completely by P28, consistent with axon outgrowth plus off-target synapse removal. Preference for axon initial segments develops before cartridge morphology.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest that connectomic screening may prove useful for future studies of experimental interference with genetic and environmental conditions of circuit formation in the mammalian brain.

summaries.beginner: Inhibitory cells in baby mouse cortex do not all wire up on the same schedule. Some already pick the right dendritic targets at five days of age, while others refine contacts onto cell bodies and axon starts over the following weeks.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2020), Gour and colleagues used 13 three-dimensional electron-microscopy datasets from mouse somatosensory layers 4 and 2/3 at postnatal days 5–56 to map inhibitory innervation of apical dendrites, somata, and axon initial segments. Apical-dendrite targeting is already near adult specificity at P5. Soma preference rises gradually, with a large shift between P7 and P9 (almost threefold preference increase and almost twofold drop in synapse density along those axons), suggesting overabundance then removal. Chandelier and axon-initial-segment preference appears by P14 and is almost complete by P28, reaching about 50% of axon-initial-segment synaptic input, before full cartridge morphology.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Exact neuron and synapse counts per age are not given. “Almost threefold” and “almost twofold” are the only quantitative developmental changes stated. The study is mouse somatosensory cortex, not human tissue.

plain_language_summary: Inhibitory cells in baby mouse cortex do not all wire up on the same schedule. Some already pick the right dendritic targets at five days of age, while others refine contacts onto cell bodies and axon starts over the following weeks.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics is motivated as predicting function from anatomy. C. elegans is the most mature connectome and is used to constrain models, so it is a place to test that claim explicitly.
ocar.challenge: Anatomy leaves sign, strength, timescales, and operational status of connections ambiguous. Extrasynaptic signaling is invisible in the connectome.
ocar.action: Randi, Sharma, Dvali, and Leifer, on arXiv (2022), systematically measure signal propagation in 23,427 neuron pairs across the C. elegans head by optogenetic activation and simultaneous whole-brain calcium imaging, building a functional atlas of sign, strength, temporal properties, and causal direction.
ocar.resolution: Signal propagation differs from anatomy-based predictions. Mutant experiments show that extrasynaptic signaling not visible from anatomy contributes to the difference. Many dense-core-vesicle-dependent signals on seconds-or-less timescales evoke acute calcium transients, often where no direct wired connection exists but relevant neuropeptides and receptors are expressed. The measured atlas better predicts spontaneous-activity dynamics than anatomy. The authors conclude that synaptic and extrasynaptic signaling both drive neural dynamics on short timescales.
ocar.future_work: Discussion flags a search for latent connections that appear only in certain internal states. The map is a lower bound because of dim identification tags, hard-to-identify neurons, and nuclear calcium imaging. Future measurements should explore a larger stimulation space, including simultaneous multi-neuron stimulation, and unrestrained freely moving worms. Inferring direct connections from effective ones may require higher signal-to-noise. Peptidergic extrasynaptic signaling may be less fast, strong, or spatially extensive in larger mammalian brains.
